analogy.p: Writing '3 × a' as 3a is like texting 'LOL' instead of 'laughing out loud': it is a shared shortcut, but only works if both sides know the code. Just as 'CU' can be read as 'see you', ab is read as 'a times b'. Powers are like a repeat sign in music: a³ is shorthand for 'a, a, a' without writing it out. The analogy breaks down because text shorthand varies from person to person, whereas algebra notation has strict, universal rules, and ordering mistakes (such as 3x² versus (3x)²) change the maths, not just the style.
analogy.t: Algebra notation is like text-message shorthand

bullets: A **variable** is a letter that can take different values (for example x in y = 2x + 1); a **constant** is a fixed number such as 7 or π.
Algebra lets us write a **general rule** (such as area = length × width) instead of lots of separate calculations.
The conventions are not optional style choices: Edexcel mark schemes expect answers in **simplified standard notation**, e.g. 6x² not 3x × 2x.
Reading notation is as important as writing it: ab means a × b, while a + b is a sum, and a/b means a ÷ b.
If a question gives you a letter with no multiplication sign next to a bracket or another letter, **always assume multiplication**.
Understanding notation is the foundation for every later algebra topic: expanding, factorising, solving, rearranging and graphs.
core.h: What algebra notation is and why it exists
core.p: Algebra uses **letters to stand for numbers** that are unknown or can change, so that one rule can describe infinitely many situations. To keep this short and unambiguous, mathematicians follow agreed **notation conventions**: we leave out multiplication signs, write repeated multiplication as powers, and write division as fractions. The Edexcel specification asks you to **use and interpret algebraic notation**, which means you must be able to both write expressions in this standard form and read them back into words and numbers. Marks in exams are often lost not because the maths is hard but because notation is misread (for example reading 3x² as (3x)²).

bullets: The number (the **coefficient**) is written before the letters: 5xy, not xy5.
a × 1 = a, so we never write 1a; and 1 × a is just a. Similarly −1 × a = **−a**.
Order does not change the value, ab = ba, but put letters in alphabetical order to be tidy and to make like terms easy to spot.
3 × 4 stays as 3 × 4 (or 12) because 34 would be read as thirty-four.
A number multiplied by a bracket also drops the sign: 5 × (x + 2) = **5(x + 2)**.
When you simplify, multiply numbers together first: 3a × 4b = (3 × 4) × a × b = **12ab**.
core.p: When two letters or a number and a letter are multiplied, **we do not write the × sign**. So a × b is written ab, and 3 × a is written 3a. By convention the **number goes first** and letters are written in **alphabetical order**, so we write 4ab rather than b4a or a4b. Multiplication is commutative (order does not matter), so ab = ba, but the standard form is the alphabetical one. The × sign is kept only between numbers (like 3 × 4) or where leaving it out would cause confusion.

bullets: a² = a × a. It is **not** 2 × a. For example if a = 5 then a² = 25, but 2a = 10.
a³ = a × a × a; a⁴ = a × a × a × a, and so on.
The power affects **only the symbol it is attached to**: 3x² means 3 × x × x, whereas (3x)² means 3x × 3x = **9x²**.
In xy² only y is squared; in (xy)² both are, giving x²y².
A letter on its own has an **invisible power of 1**: x = x¹.
Squaring a negative gives a positive: (−4)² = 16, but −4² (with no brackets) means −(4²) = **−16**.
Powers are done **before** multiplication in the order of operations, which is why 3x² means 3 × (x²).
core.h: Writing powers (indices): a², a³ and ab²
core.p: When the **same letter is multiplied by itself**, we use a power (also called an index or exponent). a × a = a² (said 'a squared'), a × a × a = a³ ('a cubed'), and in general a × a × ... × a (n times) = aⁿ. The small raised number tells you **how many copies of the base are multiplied**, not what you multiply by. The power applies **only to the thing directly in front of it**: in 2ab² the power 2 belongs to b alone, so 2ab² = 2 × a × b × b. To make a power apply to a whole product you must use brackets, as in (2ab)² = 2ab × 2ab = 4a²b².

bullets: a ÷ b = **a/b**; (a + b) ÷ 2 = **(a + b)/2**, which is NOT the same as a + b/2.
x ÷ 2 can be written as **x/2** or **½x**; both mean one half of x.
Write **fractions, not decimals**, for coefficients in algebra: ⅔x not 0.666...x.
a/b ≠ b/a unless a = b: order matters in division.
A fraction line means 'divide', so 6x/3 = 2x (divide the 6 by the 3).
Division by zero is **not possible**, so the denominator of a fraction can never be 0.
On a calculator you must put brackets around a numerator or denominator that has more than one term.
core.p: In algebra we do not use the ÷ sign. Instead, **a ÷ b is written as a fraction a/b**, with the top (numerator) divided by the bottom (denominator). The fraction bar also acts like a **pair of brackets**: in (a + b)/c, the whole of a + b is divided by c. When there is a **fractional coefficient**, Edexcel prefers it written as a fraction rather than a decimal, so we write ½x or x/2 rather than 0.5x, and 3x/4 rather than 0.75x. This keeps answers exact and avoids rounding.

bullets: Each term **includes the sign in front of it**: in 5x² − 3x + 7 the terms are 5x², **−3x** and **+7**.
The coefficient of x in 7 − 4x is **−4**, not 4, because the sign belongs to the term.
The coefficient of x in x² + x is 1 (a letter alone has coefficient 1).
**Like terms** have exactly the same letters raised to the same powers: 3ab and −5ba are like terms; 3a and 3a² are not.
Only like terms can be added or subtracted: 3x + 2x = 5x, but 3x + 2y cannot be simplified.
A **factor** divides exactly: x and 3 are factors of 3x; every term in an expression may share a **common factor**, which is used when factorising.
A **constant** has no variable part; its value never changes.
An expression with one term is a monomial, two terms a binomial, three terms a trinomial (extra vocabulary, rarely asked).
core.p: An **expression** is built from **terms**. A term is a number, a letter, or numbers and letters multiplied together (or divided), and terms are separated by + or − signs. In the term 5x² the **coefficient** is 5 (the number multiplying the letters), the **variable** is x, and the **index** is 2. A term with no letter, such as +7, is a **constant term**. A **factor** is something that divides exactly into a term: the factors of 6x include 1, 2, 3, 6, x, 2x, 3x and 6x. Precise vocabulary is rewarded because many questions say 'write down the coefficient of x' or 'state the number of terms'.

bullets: **Expression**: 3x + 5. Simplify it, expand it, factorise it, or evaluate it for a given x. You cannot 'solve' an expression.
**Equation**: 3x + 5 = 20. Only x = 5 makes it true, so you solve it.
**Formula**: v = u + at or A = πr². It connects real quantities and can be rearranged or substituted into.
**Identity**: 2(x + 3) ≡ 2x + 6 is true for all x. 'Show that' and 'prove' questions ask you to demonstrate an identity.
An **inequality** compares using <, >, ≤ or ≥ (e.g. x + 2 > 7) and has a range of solutions.
A quick test: if you can substitute **any** number and both sides always match, it is an identity; if only some numbers work, it is an equation.
A **function** is a rule that gives one output for each input, e.g. f(x) = 3x + 5 (links to the later 'functions' topic).
In the exam, writing 'the expression' when it is really an equation can cost the communication mark in a written explanation.
core.p: These four words look similar but mean different things, and the specification explicitly asks you to **understand and use the vocabulary** of expressions, equations, formulae, identities, inequalities, terms and factors. An **expression** has no equals sign and can only be simplified or evaluated. An **equation** says two things are equal and is true only for particular values of the letter, which you find by solving it. A **formula** is a rule linking quantities (with an equals sign, usually with a single subject on the left) used by substituting values. An **identity** is true **for every value** of the variable and is written with the symbol ≡, for example 2(x + 3) ≡ 2x + 6.

bullets: 'A number plus 5' = n + 5; 'five more than a number' = **n + 5**.
'Three less than a number' = **n − 3** (NOT 3 − n).
'Twice a number' = 2n; 'a number squared' = n²; 'half of a number' = n/2.
'The sum of x and y, all multiplied by 4' = **4(x + y)**; the brackets matter.
**Consecutive integers**: n, n + 1, n + 2; consecutive even numbers: 2n, 2n + 2, 2n + 4; odd numbers: 2n + 1, 2n + 3.
'Per' means divide or multiply by a rate: £12 per hour for h hours = **12h**.
Perimeter of a rectangle with width w and length (w + 3) is 2w + 2(w + 3) = **4w + 6**.
Check your expression by testing it with a simple number to see whether it behaves as the situation describes.
core.p: A common exam skill is converting a **worded situation into an expression or formula**. Choose a letter to stand for the unknown, then translate each phrase carefully, remembering that 'less than' and 'more than' reverse the order you read them. Always state what your letter means (for example 'let n be the number of tickets') when forming a formula. Building expressions is how you later set up equations to solve, and ties directly into problem-solving questions about perimeters, ages and costs.

bullets: Work out **brackets first**, including anything inside a fraction's numerator or denominator.
Then **indices** (powers and roots): in 3x² with x = 4, find 4² = 16 **before** multiplying by 3, giving 48 (not 12² = 144).
Then **division and multiplication** from left to right: 12 ÷ 3 × 2 = 4 × 2 = **8** (not 12 ÷ 6).
Then **addition and subtraction** left to right: 10 − 4 + 3 = 6 + 3 = **9**.
Treat the fraction bar as brackets: (12 + 6)/3 = 18/3 = 6.
Roots and powers count as indices; a square root sign covers everything under it.
Write each step on a new line in an exam, so a small slip can still earn **method marks**.
core.p: Whenever you substitute or simplify, you must follow the **order of operations**: **B**rackets, **I**ndices (powers and roots), **D**ivision and **M**ultiplication (left to right, equal priority), then **A**ddition and **S**ubtraction (left to right, equal priority). Many errors in substitution come from doing the steps in the wrong order, or from forgetting that an invisible multiplication sits between a number and a letter. The order exists so that everyone interprets the same expression in the same way and gets the same answer.

bullets: Step 1: write the expression or formula; Step 2: replace every letter by its value in brackets; Step 3: evaluate with BIDMAS; Step 4: write the final answer (with units if given).
Example: 4a + 3b with a = 2, b = 5 gives 4 × 2 + 3 × 5 = 8 + 15 = **23**.
Example: x² + 3x with x = 4 gives 16 + 12 = **28**.
5x with x = 3 is 15, not 53: **juxtaposition means multiplication**.
The same letter takes the same value everywhere in a question; different letters may take different values.
When the answer should be a decimal, follow the instruction (e.g. 'give your answer to 1 decimal place'), otherwise keep fractions exact.
Show the substituted line in the exam: it is usually where the method mark is.
core.h: Substituting positive numbers step by step
core.p: **Substitution** means replacing each letter with its given number, then evaluating using BIDMAS. The most reliable method is to **rewrite the expression with the numbers in brackets**, then work out powers, then multiplications, then additions. Remember that 5x means 5 × x, so if x = 3 it means 5 × 3 = 15 and **not** 53. In a formula, substitute into the right-hand side and then state the value of the subject with its **units**.

bullets: Subtracting a negative adds: 5 − (−2) = **5 + 2 = 7**. Hence 5 − y with y = −2 is 7.
Negative times negative is positive: −4 × −3 = **12**; negative times positive is negative: −4 × 3 = **−12**.
Odd powers of a negative number stay negative ((−2)³ = −8); even powers are positive ((−2)⁴ = 16).
If an answer is a negative number, keep the minus sign and include units when relevant.
Calculator: use the (−) key or brackets; type **(−2)²** as a bracket to get 4.
core.p: Negative substitutions are the biggest source of lost marks. **Always put a negative value in brackets** when you substitute. Then use the sign rules: a negative times a negative is a positive, a negative times a positive is a negative. Powers need extra care: (−3)² = 9 because the bracket means −3 is squared, but −3² is −(3 × 3) = −9. Likewise, in the expression −x² with x = 3 the answer is −9, while (−x)² with x = 3 gives (−3)² = 9.

bullets: Calculate under the root sign **first**, then take the root of the total, not the roots separately.
Check the denominator does not equal 0: that would make the expression undefined.
Keep full calculator accuracy until the end and round **only the final answer**.
Give exact answers (fractions, surds, π) when the question says 'exact' or 'leave in terms of π'.
If a question gives a value of a letter in a calculation chain, the earlier answer can be reused – read carefully for 'use your answer to part (a)'.
core.h: Substituting into fractions, roots and several-variable expressions
core.p: Many formulae include **fractions, square roots or several letters at once**. For fractions, work out the **numerator and denominator separately** (treat each as in brackets), then divide. For roots, evaluate what is under the root sign first, then take the root. On a calculator, use the fraction key or enter brackets around the top and bottom, otherwise the machine may divide only the last term. Check that the answer is sensible, for instance a length should not be negative.

bullets: **v = u + at**: final speed = initial speed + acceleration × time. u = −4, a = 3, t = 5 → v = −4 + 15 = **11**.
In ½at², the ½ multiplies a **and** t², and t² is worked out before multiplying.
Always give units: if the question says metres per second, write m/s.
core.h: Formulae in science and real life
core.p: The specification specifically mentions substituting into **scientific formulae**. Formulae appear in physics, chemistry and everyday contexts, and the skill is always the same: replace the letters by the given values, follow BIDMAS and give the answer with the correct unit. Be sure each value is in the units the formula expects. Common formulae include v = u + at, s = ut + ½at², v² = u² + 2as, F = ma, KE = ½mv², density = mass ÷ volume, speed = distance ÷ time, C = 2πr and A = πr². Edexcel will give the formula in the question when it is not one you must recall.

bullets: Taxi with a £3.50 fixed charge plus £1.20 per mile: **C = 3.5 + 1.2m**. For 7 miles, C = 3.5 + 8.4 = **£11.90**.
Fixed part + variable part: C = (fixed) + (rate × quantity).
Always **define your letters** (m = number of miles, C = cost in pounds).
Test with m = 0: the cost is the fixed charge £3.50, which is sensible.
Perimeter formulas: rectangle P = 2l + 2w = **2(l + w)**.
A formula can be written in words, e.g. 'total = 35 + 28 × hours'; the algebraic version is **T = 35 + 28h**.
Using a formula backwards (given T, find h) means forming and solving an equation: 119 = 35 + 28h → h = **3**.
core.p: To **form a formula**, read the situation, identify the quantities, choose letters, and describe how they combine. A fixed charge is a constant; a charge per unit multiplies the variable. After forming it, **test it with a simple value** to make sure it matches the situation, which is also a good way to spot a missing bracket. Forming a formula is the first step in many problem-solving questions, and the same formula can later be rearranged to find any variable.

bullets: To **show** an identity: simplify one side (or both) until they match, writing each step.
To **disprove**: substitute a value that makes the two sides different (a counterexample).
Checking one value (like x = 2) is a good **check** for an expansion, but is not a proof.
'Show that' means the answer is given: your marks come from the **working**, so do not skip lines.
Use the identity sign ≡ when stating that something is true for every value; = is fine for equations.
Typical proof: consecutive integers n and n + 1 have sum 2n + 1, which is always odd.
Even numbers can be written 2n, odd numbers 2n + 1 – useful in algebraic proof questions.
core.h: Identities, 'show that' and testing a claim
core.p: An **identity** is true for all values, and a 'show that' question asks you to prove it using algebra, not by testing numbers. **Substituting a number can disprove a claim but cannot prove it**, because one example proves nothing about all values. To disprove, one **counterexample** is enough. For instance, 2(x + 3) = 2x + 3 is false because x = 1 gives 8 on the left and 5 on the right. Good algebraic proof starts from one side, shows each step, and ends at the other side or at the same simplified expression.

bullets: **Sequences**: the nth term 3n + 2, substituting n = 1, 2, 3 gives 5, 8, 11.
**Graphs**: y = x² − 3x with x = −1 gives 1 + 3 = 4, so (−1, 4) lies on the curve – a table of values is repeated substitution.
**Rearranging formulae** (next topic) builds directly on correct notation and form.
**Ratio, speed, density and compound measures** all use formulae to substitute into.
**Higher**: algebraic proof such as 'prove the sum of three consecutive integers is a multiple of 3': n + (n + 1) + (n + 2) = 3n + 3 = 3(n + 1).
In the exam always keep your letter usage consistent and state what letters mean.
core.h: Links to other topics and Higher tier extensions
core.p: Notation and substitution run through the whole course. Substituting values into the formula for the nth term leads to sequences; substituting x-values into y = mx + c produces coordinates for straight-line graphs; substituting into formulae from other subjects (physics, geography, chemistry) is the same skill. At Higher tier you need confidence with **surds and π in formulae**, with larger formulas involving fractions and roots, and with **algebraic proof** using the vocabulary of identities.

exam: **Command words**: 'Write down' (1 mark, no working needed), 'Work out' / 'Calculate' (show working), 'Find the value of' (substitute), 'Simplify' (collect and use notation), 'Show that' (given answer; every step must be visible).
**Substitution questions** are usually 2 or 3 marks: 1 mark for correct substitution (shown), 1 for correct evaluation, sometimes 1 for the final accurate answer with units.
Always **rewrite with the values in brackets** before evaluating, especially negatives: writing the substituted line protects the method mark.
For **'write an expression' (1 or 2 marks)** define a letter if none is given and use proper notation (3n + 2, not n3 + 2 or 'three n plus 2').
For **'Show that' (2 to 3 marks)** start from a line given in the question, no skipping steps, finish with the exact target statement.
**Identity vs equation** questions: 'Is this an identity? Give a reason' – test a value that fails, or expand to show both sides match.
**Formula questions in context** need units in the final line: £, cm², m/s, J.
Spend the last minute **re-checking signs**; negatives are the commonest source of lost marks.
On **calculator papers (Papers 2 and 3)** use brackets for fractions; on **non-calculator Paper 1** write intermediate numbers carefully.
For 'give your answer to 3 significant figures' etc., keep unrounded values until the final step.
Edexcel often puts substitution into **a sequence, a graph or a physics-type formula**, so be ready to read any formula as a recipe.

mistakes.r: The power applies only to x: 3x² = 3 × x × x. For x = 2 it is 12, not 36.
mistakes.w: Writing 3x² as (3x)² = 9x², or squaring the 3 as well.

mistakes.r: x ÷ 2 = x/2; the fraction line covers the whole numerator: (a + b)/2.
mistakes.w: Writing x ÷ 2 as 2/x or a + b/2 for (a + b)/2.

mistakes.r: Write fractional coefficients as fractions: ½x or x/2.
mistakes.w: Using decimal coefficients like 0.5x in answers.
Doing addition before multiplication when substituting, e.g. 2 + 3x with x = 4 → 5 × 4 = 20.

mistakes.r: An expression has no equals sign; you simplify it. An equation can be solved.
mistakes.w: Calling an equation an expression or vice versa, or trying to 'solve' an expression.

mistakes.r: One example cannot prove; use algebra. One counterexample can disprove.
mistakes.w: Using one numerical example to 'prove' an identity.

summary: You must use and interpret algebraic notation (ab, a², a/b, brackets, coefficients as fractions), understand the vocabulary of expressions, equations, formulae, identities, inequalities, terms and factors, and substitute numbers into expressions and formulae, including scientific ones. It matters because every later algebra topic and many science and problem-solving questions rely on reading and evaluating formulae accurately.

A collection of terms with no equals sign, e.g. 3x + 5.
A statement that two expressions are equal, true only for certain values of the variable.
A rule written in algebra that links quantities, used by substituting values.
An equation that is true for all values of the variables, written with the symbol ≡.
A statement comparing expressions using <, >, ≤ or ≥.
The small raised number showing how many times the base is multiplied by itself.
A number or expression that divides exactly into another.
Terms with the same letters raised to the same powers, so they can be added or subtracted.
